quotes.text: The key to understanding the route of the Exodus is to determine the location of as many of the place names mentioned in the biblical narratives as possible. As I will attempt to show shortly, two of these, Raamses of Ex. 1:11; 12:37 and elsewhere, and Baal-zephon of Ex. 14:2 have been positively identified in their ancient Egyptian setting with a high degree of probability, based on present levels of understanding of ancient geography, texts, and recent excavations in the eastern Delta region of Egypt. The identification of these two alone provides us with an enlightening and credible understanding of the route of the Israelites out of Egypt and into the Sinai wasteland. Of these two, Raamses is by far the most important. Raamses of Ex. 1:11, one of the treasure cities built up by the Israelite slaves for the Egyptian Pharaoh, and of Ex. 12:37, the point of debarkation for the escaping Israelites, is generally assumed to have been the same as Egyptian Pi-Ramesse, the alternate Egyptian capital built during the 19th Dynasty by Rameses II, to serve as capital of Egypt along with the traditional city of Memphis. A second basic assumption of scholarship is that Rameses built his Delta capital on the same location as the by then long-abandoned Hyksos capital of Avaris. Scholars have for many years debated over which of the many tells (ruin mounds) of the eastern Delta hides the remains of Avaris and of Raamses. Until just recently the choice had largely rested on Tell san el-Hagar, ancient Tanis, known in the Bible as Zoan (Num. 13:32, Ps. 78:12). Tanis, perhaps the largest and most impressive ruin mound in Egypt, is located on the Tanitic branch of the Nile, directly west of the swampy area known as Lake Manzala. The fame of Tanis as the probable location of Avaris and of Pi-Ramesse was due to the success its early excavator, Pierre Montet, had in excavating numerous monuments at the site that could be identified from their inscriptions as having originated in Avaris and in Pi-Ramesse. For some years though, the alternate view has persisted as a minority opinion, that the Hyksos and Rameside monuments found at Tanis had been transported there from the great sites of Tell el-Daba/Qantir, just eleven miles to the south, and that this great complex of ruin mounds should rather be given the honor of hiding the remains of these great cities.
quotes.attr: JOHN M. LUNDQUIST in Kent P. Jackson and Robert L. Millet, eds., Studies in Scripture, Vol. 3: Genesis to 2 Samuel, p.115-116

quotes.text: Pithom and Raamses Both names are well known in Egyptian sources, but their precise location has not been fixed. Pithom is never again mentioned in the Bible. The name derives from the Egyptian pr/pi-'tm, which means "the House of Atum," indicating the presence of a major temple dedicated to the primeval creator god of that name. Obviously, several localities could have borne such a designation, but the site of Tell el-Maskuta in Wadi Tumeilat in the northeastern Delta of the Nile is regarded by many authorities as being the most likely candidate for the city. Raamses can be none other than the famous Delta residence of the pharaoh Ramses II; its beauty and glory were extolled in poems still extant. The city was situated in "the region of Goshen," a phrase that is synonymous with "the region of Rammses," where the Israelites lived. This is described as being "the choicest part of the land of Egypt.'" It was here that the Israelites assembled in preparation for the Exodus." The precise site has not yet been located, but Egyptologists believe that it is the region of modern el-Khata`na and Qantur in the northeastern Delta.

quotes.text: Pithom' is Egyptian - 'House of [the god Atum ... This city is known to have been a center of the cult of Atum." (Sarna, Exploring Exodus, p.20) "Atum (or Tern or Turn) was an early god of Heliopolis and a predynastic sun-diety. The Heliopolitan theologians interpret his name to be 'complete one', a reference to the belief that he created himself out of the waters of Nun by an effort of will or by the power of the spoken word - by uttering his own name. They also called him Neb-er-djer, 'Lord to the Limit' or Universal God.... as creator of the gods and men and hence of the divine order in heaven and on earth, he was called Lord of the Two Lands and as such was depicted wearing the pschent the double crown of Upper and Lower Egypt, and bearing the ankh sceptre, the sign of life and symbol of royal authority.

quotes.text: Pharaoh The title is formed by a combination of two Egyptian words, per-aa, literally, "the great house." The phrase originally applied to the royal palace and court; later, during the Nineteenth Dynasty (ca. 1306-12,00 a.c.a.), it was employed as an honorific title for the reigning monarch. It is thus analogous to the present-day use of "the Palace" or "the White House.

quotes.text: Faced with a conflict between the laws of God and those of the pharaoh, the midwives followed the dictates of conscience. Their defiance of tyranny constitutes history's first recorded act of civil disobedience in defense of a moral imperative. It is stated that they were actuated by "fear of God," a phrase frequently associated with moral and ethical behavior. "Fear of God" connotes a conception of God as One who makes moral demands on humankind; it functions as the ultimate restraint on evil and the supreme stimulus for good.

quotes.text: The oppressive acts of the pharaoh have built to a climax. Strangely, his third and most barbarous decree-infanticide-is never again referred to in the Bible. We are not told to what extent it was implemented or whether it was later rescinded. The primary function served by its narration is to set the stage for the story of the birth and survival of Moses. His arrival gives new direction to the life of the suffering people. The unseen hand of God is at work so that the king's crowning evil actually initiates a series of events that is to culminate in the humiliation of its perpetrator and the liberation of Israel.
quotes.speaker: Nahum Sarna

quotes.text: All else having failed, the pharaoh promulgates one last genocidal decree. He mobilizes "all his people," the entire apparatus of the state, to annihilate the people of Israel. There is subtle irony in his decree, for the chosen instrument of destruction-water-will in the end become the agency of Egypt's punishment.
